options: Short takeoff and landing capability
Vertical takeoff and landing capability
Short takeoff but only vertical landing
Supersonic takeoff and landing capability
questions.explanation: STOL refers to the ability to take off and land using a short distance under the stated operating criteria.

options: Short takeoff and landing only
Vertical takeoff and landing
Vertical takeoff with no provision for landing
Conventional takeoff followed by a short landing only
questions.explanation: A VTOL aircraft can take off and land vertically when operating within its limits.

questions.stem: What changes orientation in a tiltrotor aircraft?
options: The whole wing while its rotors remain fixed relative to it
The fuselage while the wing remains horizontal
The rotor and its associated nacelle
Only the rotor blades pitch while the nacelles remain fixed
questions.explanation: A tiltrotor changes the orientation of its rotor/nacelle assembly between different flight regimes.

options: Only its rotor blades change pitch; the wing stays fixed.
Its nacelles tilt while the wing remains fixed.
Its entire fuselage must rotate relative to the wing.
Its wing changes orientation relative to the fuselage.
questions.explanation: A tiltwing changes the wing orientation to support different flight conditions.

options: Changing the direction in which thrust acts
Changing thrust magnitude while keeping its direction fixed
Changing wing camber to vary aerodynamic lift
Changing the centre of gravity by moving fuel
questions.explanation: Thrust vectoring directs the thrust force rather than keeping its direction fixed.

questions.stem: Why can transition be challenging for a vertical-flight aircraft?
options: Lift and thrust remain unchanged throughout transition.
The direction of the thrust is irrelevant to control.
The lift and thrust contributions change as its flight condition changes.
Only the landing gear needs to be controlled during transition.
questions.explanation: Transition changes the balance of aerodynamic and propulsive forces and requires stable control throughout.

questions.stem: What happens to induced drag when a wing operates close to the ground in ground effect?
options: It increases because the wingtip vortices become stronger.
It can decrease relative to flight far from the ground.
It remains identical at the same lift under all heights.
It disappears at every height below one wingspan.
questions.explanation: Ground effect changes the wing flow and can reduce induced drag when the wing is close to the surface.

questions.stem: What mainly supports an air-cushion vehicle?
options: Buoyancy from a deeply submerged hull alone
Lift from a fixed wing operating far above the surface
Hydrodynamic lift from submerged foils alone
A region of air at a pressure above the surrounding air
questions.explanation: An air-cushion vehicle is supported by slightly pressurised air beneath it, usually retained in part by a skirt.

questions.stem: What does a hydrofoil do as a suitable craft gains speed?
options: Lifts the hull partly out of the water
Supports the craft mainly with a cushion of pressurised air
Keeps the hull at the same depth independently of speed
Produces lift mainly by directing engine thrust downwards
questions.explanation: Hydrodynamic lift from the foil can raise the hull and reduce its contact with the water.

questions.stem: Which condition can unexpectedly reduce clearance and increase contact risk near the surface?
options: An increase in clearance above the surface
Waves or gusts
Calmer air and a smoother surface
Reducing wave height and wind gusts
questions.explanation: Close-to-surface operation leaves limited clearance, so waves and gusts can affect stability and safety.
